title: Piloting the World's First Double-Blind AI Evaluations
hook: Benchmarks only mean something if the model hasn't seen the answers. DeepMind's pilot hides the test from the lab and the weights from the evaluators — enforced by cryptography, not a contract.
key_points: DeepMind calls it the first double-blind evaluation of a proprietary frontier-class model.
Runs inside Google Cloud Confidential Computing: evaluators can't read the weights, Google can't read the prompts.
Targets benchmark contamination — 'peeking' at eval questions inflates scores and erodes trust.
Replaces contractual promises about test-set secrecy with technical enforcement.
Piloted on a Gemini Flash Lite model with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, OpenMined, AVERI, and MLCommons.
content_html: Google DeepMind says it has run the first double-blind evaluation of a proprietary, frontier-class AI model — a pilot built with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, OpenMined, AVERI, and MLCommons, tested on a Gemini Flash Lite model. The setup fixes a structural weakness in AI benchmarking: whoever holds the test set has to be trusted not to leak it, and whoever holds the model has to be trusted not to look.
extra_html:
How it works

The evaluation runs inside Google Cloud's Confidential Computing environment — a cryptographic "box" that both parties feed inputs into but neither can see inside. External evaluators never get access to the model weights; Google never gets to see the test prompts. Both sides get the result, and neither is in a position to game it.

Why it matters

Benchmark contamination is one of the quieter credibility problems in AI evaluation. As the post frames it, if models can "peek" at the evaluation questions in advance, it "can artificially inflate scores and undermine this trust." Until now the defense has largely been contractual — a lab promising it didn't train on the test set. Making that guarantee technical rather than legal is what's new here, and it matters most for third-party safety evaluations, where the evaluator and the developer have reasons not to simply trust each other. DeepMind published an accompanying technical report with the methodology and findings.

related.title: Separating Signal from Noise in Coding Evaluations
related.hook: OpenAI told the field to switch to SWE-Bench Pro after finding SWE-bench Verified contaminated. Now its own audit says ~30% of SWE-Bench Pro's tasks are broken too.

related.title: Model Evaluation for Extreme Risks
related.hook: General-purpose AI tends to pick up dangerous capabilities alongside useful ones. So test for those capabilities directly — before you ship, not after.

flashcards.back_html: Neither side sees the other's secret: evaluators can't access the model's weights, and the model's developer can't see the test prompts.

flashcards.prompt: What problem is double-blind evaluation primarily designed to prevent?

choices.text: Benchmark contamination — the model having seen the eval questions in advance
Evaluators running the model on too little compute
Models refusing to answer safety questions
Benchmarks becoming too difficult over time

flashcards.explanation_html: DeepMind's framing: if models can 'peek' at evaluation questions beforehand, scores are artificially inflated and the trust the benchmark is supposed to create disappears.

flashcards.prompt: What replaces the contract in this setup, and how?
flashcards.back_html: Technical enforcement. Confidential Computing puts the evaluation in a cryptographic box, so test-set secrecy no longer depends on either party keeping a promise.
